entry: Stage of the English language spoken in England from the [[Norman Conquest]] of 1066 until the late 15th century. Middle English evolved from [[Old English]] under the influence of Anglo-Norman French and Old Norse. Most grammatical case distinctions were reduced and eventually lost, and the language came to depend more on word order. Its vocabulary absorbed many Anglo-Norman words, especially in politics, law, the arts and religion. Regional dialects differed widely; the four main dialects in England were Northern, East Midland, West Midland and Southern. By about 1470 a standard based on London dialects, the Chancery Standard, had become established. Aided by the printing press, invented by [[Johannes Gutenberg]] in 1439, it formed the basis for [[Modern English]] spelling. The period's most studied work is *The Canterbury Tales* by [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]. In England, Middle English was succeeded by Early Modern English, which lasted until about 1650.

Period of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptian]] history, approximately 2040 to 1782 or 1700 BC, depending on the definition, between the First and Second Intermediate Periods. Mentuhotep II, who ruled from Thebes, reunified Egypt after a long period of division and is regarded as the founder of the Middle Kingdom. He campaigned as far south as the Second Cataract in [[Nubia]], restored Egyptian control over the Sinai, and depicted himself as a god wearing the headdresses of [[Amun]] and Min. Mentuhotep III sent the first expedition to Punt during the Middle Kingdom, using ships built at the end of Wadi Hammamat on the [[Red Sea]]. Osiris became the most important deity in popular religion. The idea of the Middle Kingdom as one of three golden ages was coined in 1845 by the German Egyptologist Baron von Bunsen. It was followed by the Second Intermediate Period, when the Hyksos of West Asia ruled Lower Egypt.

Second subdivision of the [[Paleolithic]], or Old [[Stone Age]], as understood in Europe, Africa and Asia. It broadly spanned 300,000 to 50,000 years ago and was succeeded by the [[Upper Paleolithic]]. The earliest evidence of [[Behavioral modernity|behavioral modernity]] first appears in this period, although undisputed evidence becomes common only in the Upper Paleolithic. The earliest undisputed artistic expression includes bracelets, beads and [[Ochre|ochre]] used as body paint, at sites such as Blombos Cave. Burials at Krapina in Croatia and at the Qafzeh and Es Skhul caves in Israel have led some scholars to suggest religious beliefs, including an afterlife, though others attribute them to secular reasons. Long-distance trade in raw materials began as early as 120,000 years ago. According to the recent African origin theory, anatomically modern humans began migrating out of [[Africa]] around 125,000 years ago and replaced other Homo species, including [[Neanderthal|Neanderthals]].

Phase of adulthood between young adulthood and old age, commonly defined as ages 40 to 64. Definitions vary, and many people now place its start near age 55. Physical changes include graying hair and a decline in fertility, and women typically experience [[Menopause|menopause]] between ages 45 and 55. Mortality rates begin to rise, mainly because of heart problems, [[Cancer|cancer]], [[Hypertension|hypertension]] and [[Diabetes|diabetes]], although most middle-aged people in industrialized nations live into old age. [[Erik Erikson]] called this stage generativity versus stagnation, the seventh of eight stages of psychosocial development. Career satisfaction shifts toward inner contentment, and career changes remain common. The perception of a typical midlife crisis is described as largely false, though a subset of people may experience one.

Class of people in the middle of a societal hierarchy, often defined by occupation, income, education or social status. Common definitions range from the middle fifth of people on a nation's income ladder to everyone except the poorest and wealthiest 20%. In the United States the term describes people who in other countries would be called [[Working class|working class]]. The term was first attested in a 1745 pamphlet by James Bradshaw. [[Friedrich Engels]] saw the category as lying between the nobility and the peasantry in late feudal society, and the middle classes helped drive the [[French Revolution]]. The modern usage dates to the 1913 U.K. Registrar-General's report, which placed the middle class between the upper and working classes. In 2009, *The Economist* asserted that over half the world's population belonged to the middle class.

Novel by [[George Eliot]], the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, published in eight installments from December 1871 to December 1872. Subtitled *A Study of Provincial Life*, it is set in the fictional Midlands town of Middlemarch from 1829 to 1832 and follows many intersecting characters, including Dorothea Brooke, who searches for purpose, and the physician Tertius Lydgate. Its themes include the status of women, the nature of marriage, religion, hypocrisy, political reform and education. It approaches events such as the Reform Act 1832 and the early railways in a realist mode, leavened with comic elements. Its serial form borrowed a method used for Victor Hugo's *Les Misérables*. Initial reviews were mixed, but 70 years later it was considered Eliot's best work and one of the great English novels.

Small [[Fly|fly]] of any of several families of non-mosquito nematoceran Diptera. Midges are found on nearly every land area outside permanently arid deserts and the frigid zones. Some, such as sand flies and [[Black fly|black flies]], are vectors of disease. Others are prey for insectivores, including frogs and [[Swallow|swallows]]. Most midges, except the gall midges, are aquatic as larvae. Biting midges, known as no-see-ums, deliver painful bites and spread diseases such as bluetongue in livestock. The larvae of some non-biting midges contain [[Hemoglobin|hemoglobin]] and are called bloodworms.

Novel by Indian-British writer [[Salman Rushdie]], published in 1981. Its narrator, Saleem Sinai, is born at the moment of [[India]]'s independence and discovers that children born in India in the same hour have special powers. The novel is a postcolonial, magical realist story in three books, interweaving Saleem's personal history with the nation's history of colonial rule and [[Partition of India|partition]]. Saleem leads a Midnight Children's Conference that links hundreds of gifted children telepathically. Its political passages criticize [[Indira Gandhi]]'s rule during the [[The Emergency (India)|Emergency]], when Saleem is held as a political prisoner. The novel won the [[Booker Prize]] in 1981 and sold over one million copies in the UK alone. It reached number 100 in the BBC's *The Big Read* poll of the UK's best-loved novels in 2003.

Phenomenon in which the Sun remains visible at local midnight during summer, also called polar day. It occurs north of the [[Arctic Circle]] and south of the [[Antarctic Circle]], at latitudes from approximately 65°44' to the poles, and [[Refraction|refraction]] extends it slightly beyond the polar circles. At the [[North Pole]] it lasts about six months, from approximately 18 March to 24 September. [[Murmansk]], Russia, the world's largest city north of the Arctic Circle, has midnight sun from 22 May to 22 July, or 62 days. The opposite, [[Polar night]], occurs in winter when the Sun stays below the horizon all day.

U.S. atoll in the North Pacific Ocean, an unincorporated territory of the United States. Its three islands are Sand Island, the only inhabited one, Eastern Island and Spit Island, which together enclose Midway Lagoon. Midway lies about 1,310 miles northwest of [[Honolulu]] and is part of the [[Hawaiian Islands]] but not the state of [[Hawaii]]. From 1941 to 1993 it hosted a naval air facility that played a role in the [[Battle of Midway]] (June 4–6, 1942), a critical Allied victory and a turning point of the Pacific campaign of [[World War II]]. Today the atoll is a national wildlife refuge managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and about 50 people live on Sand Island, mostly as staff and contractors.

One of four census regions of the United States, occupying the northern central part of the country. Also called the Midwest or the Heartland, it comprises 12 states: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota and Wisconsin. The 2020 U.S. census put its population at 68,995,685. The region lies on the broad Interior Plain between the Appalachian and Rocky Mountains, and its major rivers include the [[Ohio River]], the upper [[Mississippi River]] and the [[Missouri River]]. [[Chicago]] is its most populous city, and its metropolitan area has an estimated 9.4 million residents. The economy mixes heavy industry and [[Agriculture|agriculture]], with extensive areas in the Corn Belt. Politically, the region includes multiple swing states and is often decisive in elections.

Duke of Poland from 960 to 992 and founder of the first unified Polish state. A member of the Piast dynasty, he was baptized in 966 and became the first Christian ruler of Poland; his 965 marriage to the Přemyslid princess Dobrawa is said to have brought the Christian faith to Poland. He extended Polish control through alliance and force, subjugating Kuyavia, waging war for Western Pomerania, and capturing Silesia and Lesser Poland late in his reign. He made alliances with [[Bohemia]], [[Sweden]] and the [[Holy Roman Empire]], and his daughter became queen consort of [[Denmark]]. He left his son [[Bolesław I the Brave]] a country with greatly expanded territories and a well-established position in Europe.

Neurological disorder that causes recurrent moderate-to-severe headaches, often on one side of the head. Attacks are generally associated with nausea, light sensitivity and sound sensitivity, and some begin with an aura, a sensory disturbance. Triggers include lack of sleep, skipped meals and hormonal fluctuations. It is believed to result from a combination of genetic, environmental and neurological factors. Mild to moderate attacks are first treated with over-the-counter pain relievers such as [[Ibuprofen|ibuprofen]] and [[Paracetamol|paracetamol]], and triptans are recommended for moderate to severe attacks. Preventive medications include beta blockers, anticonvulsants and certain antidepressants, while opioids should generally not be used. Approximately 14% (1.16 billion) of people have a migraine in a given year. Women experience more and longer migraines than men, beginning in [[Puberty|puberty]], and migraines tend to decrease after [[Menopause|menopause]].

European period of large-scale migrations, c. AD 300–600, also called the Barbarian Invasions. Tribes including the [[Vandals]], [[Goths]], Burgundians, Alemanni and [[Lombards]] migrated into and settled former Roman territories, establishing post-Roman kingdoms. Historians traditionally date the period from the invasion of Europe by the [[Huns]] in about AD 375 to the Lombard conquest of Italy in 568. Estimates for the Gothic crossing of the [[Danube]] in 376 range from 90,000–200,000 people, and total migration into Roman territory may have reached 500,000 to over 1,000,000 people. The fall of the [[Western Roman Empire]] led to competing barbarian kingdoms, while the Eastern Roman Empire survived until the [[Fall of Constantinople|fall of Constantinople]] in 1453. Scholars continue to debate whether migration or internal decline caused Rome's collapse.

Mexican Catholic priest and leader of the early phase of the [[Mexican War of Independence]]. A professor at the Colegio de San Nicolás in Valladolid, he was influenced by Enlightenment ideas, which contributed to his ouster in 1792. On the night of 15–16 September 1810, after the Conspiracy of Querétaro was discovered, he rang church bells and called the population to arms. He is widely recognized as the father of the Mexican nation for issuing the *Grito de Dolores*, which initiated the armed struggle against Spanish colonial rule. He assembled a large, poorly disciplined popular army that scored early successes in the Bajío and headed a provincial government in [[Guadalajara]]. After a decisive defeat at the Battle of Calderón Bridge in January 1811, he was captured while fleeing north, defrocked and executed by [[Execution by firing squad|firing squad]] in Chihuahua on 30 July 1811. His short leadership radicalized the independence movement and paved the way for José María Morelos.

Mexican drug lord and founder of the Guadalajara Cartel, which controlled much of Mexico's drug trafficking and the border corridors in the 1980s. He formed alliances with Colombian cartels, especially the [[Medellín Cartel]] of [[Pablo Escobar]], to smuggle drugs into the United States. Sometime in the 1980s he put Joaquín Guzmán, known as [[El Chapo]], in charge of logistics. Arrested in 1989 on charges of ordering the murder of Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena, he served a 40-year sentence and was granted house arrest in 2022.

American animator, actor and filmmaker, creator of the animated series *Beavis and Butt-Head*. Born in Guayaquil, Ecuador, and raised in [[Albuquerque, New Mexico|Albuquerque]], he worked briefly in physics and engineering before turning to animation. His short *Frog Baseball* became the [[MTV]] series *Beavis and Butt-Head*, and with Greg Daniels he created *King of the Hill*, which ran for 13 seasons on Fox. He wrote and directed *Office Space* (1999) and *Idiocracy* (2006), and he co-created the HBO series *Silicon Valley*. Judge has won a Primetime Emmy Award and two Annie Awards for *King of the Hill*.

Canadian-American actor, comedian and filmmaker, known for the title roles in the *Wayne's World*, *Austin Powers* and *Shrek* franchises. He was a cast member on [[Saturday Night Live]] from 1989 to 1995, and his work there won him a Primetime Emmy Award for writing. He played the title role in *The Cat in the Hat* (2003), a live-action adaptation of a [[Dr. Seuss]] book. He made his directorial debut with the documentary *Supermensch: The Legend of Shep Gordon* (2013) and created the [[Netflix]] series *The Pentaverate* (2022). In 2002 he received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]], and in 2017 he was named an Officer of the Order of Canada.

American film and theater director and comedian, one of 28 people to have won all four major American entertainment awards: Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony. He began in the 1950s with an improvisational troupe in Chicago and formed the comedy duo Nichols and May with Elaine May. He won Tony Awards for directing *Luv* and *The Odd Couple*, and a sixth in 2012 for a revival of [[Arthur Miller]]'s *Death of a Salesman*. He directed *Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?* (1966) and won the Academy Award for Best Director for *The Graduate* (1967). His films also include *Silkwood* (1983) and *Closer* (2004).

American former professional heavyweight boxer, widely regarded as one of the greatest heavyweights of all time. Nicknamed "Iron Mike" early in his career, he was the youngest boxer to win a heavyweight title, at age 20. He was the first heavyweight to hold the WBA, WBC and IBF titles simultaneously and held the undisputed title from 1987 to 1990, when he lost to Buster Douglas. In 1992 he was convicted of rape and sentenced to six years in prison, and he was released on parole after three years. In a 1997 rematch with [[Evander Holyfield]], he was disqualified for biting Holyfield's ears.

Russian revolutionary anarchist and political philosopher, among the most influential figures of [[Anarchism|anarchism]]. Born into a noble family in the Tver Governorate, he studied in Moscow and Berlin before meeting [[Karl Marx]] and [[Pierre-Joseph Proudhon]] in Paris, who deeply influenced him. He was expelled from France for opposing the [[Russian Empire]]'s occupation of Poland and took part in uprisings in Prague and [[Dresden]] in 1848 and 1849. Sentenced to death and extradited several times, he was exiled to Siberia, escaped and reached [[London]]. In 1868 he joined the International Workingmen's Association, where he clashed with Marx over the role of the state, and he was expelled in 1872. He founded the Anti-Authoritarian International that year. He argued that Marxist states would become one-party dictatorships, and his book *God and the State* remains in print. He influenced thinkers including [[Peter Kropotkin]].

Latvian and American dancer, choreographer and actor. Born in [[Riga]], he joined the Kirov Ballet in 1967 and became the preeminent male classical ballet dancer of the 1970s and 1980s. In 1974, while touring Toronto with the Bolshoi, he defected and requested political asylum in Canada. He joined the New York City Ballet to learn [[George Balanchine|George Balanchine]]'s neoclassical style, then danced with the American Ballet Theatre, later becoming its artistic director, and promoted [[Modern dance|modern dance]]. He starred in *The Turning Point* (1977), receiving an Academy Award nomination, and in *White Nights* (1985). He became a U.S. citizen in 1986 and never returned to the [[Soviet Union]]. Latvia granted him citizenship for extraordinary merit in 2017.

Russian and Soviet novelist and playwright. Trained as a physician, he served in rural Ukraine and during the [[Russian Civil War]] before moving to [[Moscow]] in 1921 and turning to literature. His play *The Days of the Turbins*, adapted from his novel *The White Guard*, drew official criticism for its sympathetic portrayal of White forces. The Soviet government banned many of his works, including *Flight*, which it judged to have glorified emigration and White generals. [[Joseph Stalin]] reportedly attended *The Days of the Turbins* at least 15 times and intervened on Bulgakov's behalf, yet he was only briefly successful during his lifetime. His novel *The Master and Margarita*, published posthumously in 1966–67, has been called one of the masterpieces of the 20th century.

Soviet and Russian politician, the last leader of the Soviet Union from 1985 until its dissolution in 1991. He served as general secretary of the [[Communist Party of the Soviet Union]] from 1985 and as head of state from 1988. Initially committed to [[Marxism–Leninism]], he judged reform necessary for the Soviet state's survival. He withdrew troops from the [[Soviet–Afghan War]] and held summits with U.S. president [[Ronald Reagan]] to limit nuclear weapons and end the [[Cold War]]. His policies of glasnost ("openness") and perestroika ("restructuring") allowed greater freedom of speech and the press and decentralized economic decision-making. When [[Warsaw Pact]] countries abandoned Marxist–Leninist governance in 1989, he declined to intervene militarily. A coup against him in August 1991 failed, and the Soviet Union dissolved against his wishes. Critics argue that his reforms weakened Russia's global influence and precipitated economic collapse, while he is praised for ending the Cold War. He received the Nobel Peace Prize.

Russian Romantic writer, poet and painter, sometimes called the poet of the Caucasus. Educated at home by his grandmother, he moved to [[Moscow]] in 1827 and to [[Saint Petersburg]] in 1832, where he joined the Life-Guard Hussar regiment. His poem "Death of the Poet," written after the death of [[Alexander Pushkin]] in 1837, brought him fame and his first exile to the [[Caucasus]]. There he wrote *A Hero of Our Time* (1840), whose prose founded the tradition of the Russian psychological novel. He was exiled a second time after another [[Duel|duel]]. In 1841 he was killed in a duel with fellow officer Nikolai Martynov, a death that marked the loss of one of Russia's most promising literary talents.
